criterion_notes.c1: Examines municipal delivery of free basic services to poor urban households in eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality, explicitly covering free basic water (6 kL per month) and basic sanitation/refuse removal alongside electricity.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading: under the plain wording, it examines municipal indigent policy governance and administrative implementation; under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly analyses rule-type mechanisms governing service access and tariff subsidies, including eligibility screening, property-value thresholds (R250,000 extended to R500,000), income means-testing (ZAR 1,500/month), income documentation barriers (lack of formal payslips for informal-sector workers), 24-month beneficiary review rules, and administrative maintenance/discretion in the municipal indigent register.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary qualitative empirical case study collecting semi-structured in-depth interviews from 11 purposively selected municipal employees across five eThekwini departments (including Water Services) supplemented by document review, transcribed verbatim and analysed via thematic/content analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative outcomes on access to subsidized/free basic water (6 kL/month) and municipal services, affordability relief, and administrative exclusion or mis-targeting of poor households (including exclusion of informal workers without payslips, households near property-value cutoffs, and politically unconnected poor households due to register maintenance failures and corruption). Qualitative socio-legal/administrative empirical studies are eligible without quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (municipal indigent-policy administration in eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality affecting urban indigent households; n = 11 interviewed municipal officials across five units), exposure (indigent policy eligibility criteria, means test, property-value thresholds, documentation requirements, and register administration), outcome (access to/exclusion from free basic water and municipal service subsidies), and study design (qualitative case study) are all clearly identifiable.

evidence_quotes.quote: The study adopted a qualitative data approach where a semi-structured interview was used to collect data from 11 purposively selected employees from five departments of eThekwini municipality.

For example, when you talk about water, we use the threshold of a property value if your property value is R250 000 and below you qualify automatically for free basic water up to 6 kL per month, but with the new policy that threshold has been extended to R500 000 but obviously, there are certain criteria you have to meet.

The previous policy was based on the rateable property, which specifically was based on the value of the property. The current policy that is in its early stages of execution seeks to identify and select beneficiaries based on both a property value and a means test.

This study found that given the poor maintenance of the indigent register, it usually attracts nepotism and corruption in terms of the selection of indigents, and in most cases, if the poor household is not politically connected with a person of influence, that household may not benefit.
However, the complexity encountered with regard to identifying beneficiaries as many poor households do not have proper payslips to determine their level of income as they have informal jobs.

raw_response.exposure: Municipal indigent policy rules and administrative implementation, including property-value thresholds (R250,000 extended to R500,000), household income means testing (ZAR 1,500/month), formal income documentation (payslips), 24-month re-verification rules, fragmented departmental execution, and indigent register maintenance.
raw_response.outcome: Household qualification for, affordability subsidy receipt of, and administrative exclusion from free basic municipal services, specifically including free basic water (up to 6 kL/month) and basic sanitation/solid waste collection.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban indigent households and municipal service delivery administration in eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa; qualitative interview sample of n = 11 purposively selected municipal employees across five units (3 deputy city managers, 2 Water Services staff, 2 Electricity Customer Services and Revenue Protection staff, 2 Finance – Revenue Services staff, and 2 Strategy Office staff; p. 4 also contains a parenthetical reference to n = 55 roles, while Abstract and Data collection procedures confirm 11 in-depth interviews conducted).
raw_response.rationale: This empirical qualitative case study of eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality in South Africa satisfies all systematic-review inclusion criteria (c1–c6). It examines household access to free basic water (6 kL/month) and basic sanitation/municipal services (c1) as governed by concrete legal-administrative rule mechanisms—eligibility screening, property-value tariff thresholds, income means tests, payslip documentation requirements, 24-month review rules, and indigent register administration—satisfying both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2 (c2). It presents primary qualitative empirical data from 11 semi-structured interviews with municipal officials including Water Services staff (c3), reports access, affordability-subsidy, and administrative-exclusion outcomes (c4), identifies population, exposure, outcome, and qualitative case-study design (c5), and is written in English (c6). Per review rules, qualitative socio-legal/administrative studies are included in the systematic review for mechanism synthesis even without quantitative effect estimates.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative case study (semi-structured in-depth interviews and document review with thematic and content analysis)
